passage:
Mentor's note, first-year check-ins. Vidya.
Pranav (20) came to discuss electives and ended up talking about something else. He cooks for himself now, paid his own hostel fine and chose his minor without asking anyone. But his father still pays the fees and wants weekly updates. "Am I an adult or not, ma'am? My cousin got married at twenty-one. I can't even decide if I should say I've grown up." I told him many students his age describe exactly this, and it isn't a sign he's behind. We listed which decisions are already his and which are shared for now. He seemed lighter and joked that he'd "graduated to half-adult." Next: check in after mid-semester exams; I've suggested he handle his own bank visit next month.

qa.q: What had Pranav paid for himself?
qa.a: His own hostel fine.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when he asked, "Am I an adult or not?"
qa.a: He felt confused and a little behind, comparing himself with a cousin who married at twenty-one.

qa.q: Why was listing which decisions are already his a helpful step?
qa.a: It gave him concrete proof of growing up while being honest about what is still shared, so the in-between stage feels normal, not like failure.

qa.q: How might Pranav's father see the weekly updates?
qa.a: He may see them as care and responsibility, since he pays the fees, rather than as doubting his son.

grounding: A young man who cooks and decides for himself but still depends on his father's fees feels unsure whether he is grown up, and learns this is common.

passage:
Wed, late
Signed my own rent agreement today! Actual signature, actual adult. Then called Abbu to ask if the deposit amount sounded okay. So. Half adult.
Maria says she felt the same at 22: cooked, paid bills, still got her mum to book her dentist. We laughed about it at the kitchen counter over instant noodles.
The weird part was the question at Aunty's party: "So, are you grown up now?" I didn't know what to say. I earn from tutoring, but Abbu still sends money and still calls me his little girl. I choose my own subjects, but I still cry on the train back after the holidays.
Maybe it's not a switch. Maybe it's a dimmer. Mine's about halfway. That's not failing. It's just Wednesday.
Dilnaz

qa.q: What did Dilnaz sign today?
qa.a: Her own rent agreement.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel when asked, "So, are you grown up now?"
qa.a: She felt unsure and caught between two stages, earning from tutoring but still taking money from Abbu.

qa.q: What helps Dilnaz feel better about being "half adult"?
qa.a: Hearing Maria felt the same and picturing adulthood as a dimmer, not a switch, so being halfway feels normal rather than a failure.

qa.q: How might Abbu feel when Dilnaz calls about the deposit?
qa.a: He may feel glad she still values his opinion, while noticing she is handling big things on her own now.

grounding: A young woman who signs her own lease but still leans on her father feels half adult, and comes to see the in-between as normal.

passage:
Suraj, twenty-one, ran a phone-repair counter in the market of their kasba from ten to seven, and he had chosen it himself, against his father's wish for a government exam. He paid his own counter rent. But he still slept in the room he'd had since Class 3, and every morning Ma still put a steel tiffin in his bag.
At lunch his older sister Devika, visiting from her in-laws', teased him. "So, are you a grown-up now or not?"
He opened his mouth and closed it. He had argued with a supplier alone that morning. He had also asked Papa for money for a new soldering machine last week.
"Half?" he said.
Devika laughed. "At twenty-three I cooked for six people and still phoned Ma to ask how much salt. It passes."
He wasn't sure it did. But he ate the tiffin.

qa.q: What did Ma put in Suraj's bag every morning?
qa.a: A steel tiffin.

qa.q: Why did Suraj open his mouth and close it when Devika asked if he was grown up?
qa.a: He felt torn between two answers: he runs his own counter and argues with suppliers, yet still takes money and a tiffin from home.

qa.q: What does Devika's story about the salt do for Suraj?
qa.a: It shows the in-between feeling is common, not a failure, so he needn't judge himself for answering 'Half'.

qa.q: How might Ma see Suraj's in-between stage when she packs the tiffin?
qa.a: She may still see him partly as her child to look after, while also watching him make grown-up choices at the counter.

grounding: A twenty-one-year-old who runs his own counter but still leans on his parents cannot say whether he is grown up, and hears that the feeling is common.

passage:
The laundromat on Paulo's street in Manila smelled of warm cotton. Paulo, twenty-one, folded his shirts badly while Soo-ah, from his engineering class, waited for her dryer.
"My mother sent money again today," Paulo said. "For rent. I'd told her I didn't need it."
"Did you send it back?"
"No." He creased a sleeve twice. "I chose my course, I found this flat, I cook. But she pays half the rent, and I still call her when I get a fever."
Soo-ah laughed. "My mum sends kimchi by courier, and last month I nearly cried with relief. I also signed my own lease in a foreign country. So am I a child or an adult?"
"Both. Neither."
"Everyone in our class is like this, Paulo. We just don't say it."
He folded the next shirt a little more neatly.

qa.q: What does Soo-ah's mum send by courier?
qa.a: She sends kimchi by courier.

qa.q: Why does Paulo crease the sleeve twice while talking about the money?
qa.a: He seems uneasy and a bit embarrassed at still taking help from his mother while making his own choices.

qa.q: What does Soo-ah's remark about the whole class change for Paulo?
qa.a: It shows the in-between feeling is common, not a personal failure, which seems to settle him as he folds the next shirt more neatly.

qa.q: How might Paulo's mother see sending the rent money?
qa.a: She may see it as a way of still caring for him, not as a sign that he has failed to grow up.

grounding: Two students abroad admit to feeling neither child nor adult, partly dependent yet choosing alone, and see the feeling is common.

passage:
Thursday night
Charu asked me today while we were making instant noodles in our PG kitchen, "Do you feel grown up yet?" I laughed, but it stuck.
Like: I chose my own electives this semester. I fixed the bathroom tap myself. I went to the doctor alone when I had the fever. That all feels very adult.
But Papa still sends money every month. I still call Mumma before buying anything expensive. And when the landlord shouted about the late rent, I wanted to cry and call home, not handle it.
So what am I? Twenty and half-made. Charu says she feels the same. That helped more than I expected. Maybe nobody our age feels finished. Maybe this in-between thing is just where we are right now, not something I'm failing at.
- Mahima

qa.a: Charu asked, "Do you feel grown up yet?"

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when the landlord shouted about the late rent?
qa.a: Mahima felt overwhelmed and small, wanting to cry and call home rather than deal with it.

qa.q: What helped Mahima see the in-between feeling differently?
qa.a: Hearing that Charu felt the same made it seem normal for their age rather than a personal failure.

qa.q: How might Mahima's parents see this stage?
qa.a: Mahima's parents might see a child who is growing up, still needing some support but making many choices alone.

grounding: A young adult who still depends partly on parents but makes many choices alone feels neither child nor adult, and learns the feeling is common.

passage: Jatin got off the bus in Hoshangabad with a backpack and a new beard. He was twenty-one, back from his third year in Indore, where he cooked, paid his own phone bill, and had just picked a final-year project nobody at home understood. At the gate his mother handed him a steel glass of water and told him to wash before touching anything. His little sister Arohi giggled. At dinner, Papa asked if he'd "grown up yet or still sleeping till noon." Jatin laughed, but lay awake later under the ceiling fan of his childhood room. In Indore he felt like a man making decisions. Here he felt twelve. Both felt true. In the morning Arohi, fifteen, asked him how he'd chosen his project. He explained carefully, and she listened like he was an adult. Maybe he was, a bit. Maybe that was okay.

qa.q: What town did Jatin come back to?
qa.a: Jatin came back to Hoshangabad.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling as he lay awake under the ceiling fan?
qa.a: Jatin felt confused and caught in between, like a man in Indore but like a twelve-year-old at home.

qa.q: What could help Jatin feel steadier about this stage?
qa.a: Recognising that both feelings can be true at his age, and sharing adult choices with family as he did with Arohi, could ease the sense of failing.

qa.q: How does Arohi see her brother?
qa.a: Arohi listens to him like an adult and seems to look up to him, curious how he made his choice.

grounding: A young adult feels adult in his college city but like a child at home, caught in a common in-between stage.

passage:
Sami was twenty-one, living in a shared flat in Osaka for his exchange year. He cooked his own meals, paid his own phone bill, and navigated the city alone. But his parents in Istanbul still paid his rent, and his mother still called to ask if he'd eaten.
At the izakaya, his Japanese classmate Hiroshi asked, "Do you feel like an adult?"
Sami laughed. "Some days. When I sort out a visa form alone, yes. When I call my mum because I can't figure out how to cook rice, no."
"Same," Hiroshi said. "My parents still pay my fees. But I chose my major against their wishes."
They clinked glasses. Sami felt oddly relieved. So it wasn't just him. Neither of them was fully a kid, or fully grown-up.

qa.q: Who still paid Sami's rent?
qa.a: His parents in Istanbul still paid his rent.

qa.q: How did Sami feel when Hiroshi said 'Same'?
qa.a: He felt oddly relieved, realising he wasn't the only one feeling in-between.

qa.q: What could Sami remind himself when he doubts he's grown up?
qa.a: That feeling partly adult and partly dependent is common at his age, not a failure.

qa.q: How does Hiroshi see his own in-between life?
qa.a: Hiroshi also feels in-between, relying on his parents for fees but making his own choice of major.

grounding: A young adult feels neither fully a child nor fully an adult, partly dependent and partly independent, and finds the feeling is common.

passage:
At the university hostel in Delhi, Aparna, twenty, was filling in her first tax form for her part-time tutoring job. Her mother was still sending money for her mess fees.
Her roommate Vidya looked over. "You look confused."
"I am. I decide everything alone here, what I eat, when I sleep, what course to take. But I still call Mummy when I get a fever. And she still pays for half my life."
"So are you an adult?"
Aparna put her pen down. "I don't know. I feel like I should be. Everyone expects me to be. But I'm somewhere in the middle."
Vidya shrugged. "I think we all are. It's a stage, not a failure."
Aparna smiled a little and went back to the form.

qa.q: What was Aparna filling in?
qa.a: Her first tax form for her part-time tutoring job.

qa.q: How does Aparna feel about whether she is an adult?
qa.a: She feels confused and a bit pressured, thinking she should feel adult but finding herself in the middle.

qa.q: What does Vidya's answer offer Aparna?
qa.a: Reassurance that feeling in-between is a common stage, not a failure.

qa.q: How does Vidya see the in-between feeling?
qa.a: Vidya sees it as something everyone their age goes through, a stage rather than a failure.

grounding: A young woman makes choices alone yet is partly dependent on her mother, and feels unsure whether she has grown up.

passage:
Dear Lokesh,
You asked in your last message if I "feel grown-up now" that I'm twenty-one. Honestly? I don't know.
I live in Gangtok alone, I cook, I pay my phone bill, I chose my job at the hotel without asking anyone. That feels adult.
But my father still pays my rent. I still call my mother when I'm sick. At family functions, my uncles still pinch my cheeks.
Some days I'm proud of myself. Some days I feel like a kid wearing an adult's coat.
My friends feel the same. None of us know when it happens. Maybe it's slow, not one day.
Tell me how you feel.
Pema

qa.a: In Gangtok.

qa.q: How does Pema feel about being twenty-one?
qa.a: Pema feels proud some days and like a kid wearing an adult's coat on others, unsure whether grown-up yet.

grounding: A young adult feels neither fully a child nor fully an adult, partly dependent yet choosing alone, and sees it is common.

passage: You asked if I feel like an adult. Honestly? Depends on the hour. I'm Pradeep, twenty-one. At 9 am I'm negotiating with my landlord in Hyderabad about the leaking tap, very serious, very grown-up. At 2 pm my father sends money for the rent and I feel about twelve. I choose my own courses, cook my own terrible dal, decide when I sleep. But when I got a fever last month, the first thing I did was call my mother and cry. My friend Vishal has a job already and pays for everything himself, and next to him I feel like I'm pretending. Then again, Vishal still sends his laundry home. Maybe nobody our age feels finished. I used to think this in-between feeling meant I was failing at growing up. Now I think it's just where I am.

passage:
Monday: Gargi signed her first rental agreement for a shared flat in Bengaluru, alone, reading every clause twice. She felt tall.
Thursday: her card was declined at the grocery shop; the month's money from home hadn't come yet. She put back the paneer, called Papa, and heard herself say sorry three times. She felt small, like a schoolgirl who'd lost her bus pass.
The next Sunday: on a video call, her older sister Sarika asked, 'So, are you a proper adult now?' Gargi laughed, then didn't. 'I don't know. Some days yes. Some days I want Mummy to tell me what to eat.' Sarika smiled. 'I'm twenty-six and I still call Mummy about dal. It doesn't mean you're failing.' Gargi hung up and cooked the dal badly, her own way.

qa.q: What did Gargi put back at the grocery shop?
qa.a: The paneer.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel when her card was declined?
qa.a: Gargi felt small and embarrassed, like a schoolgirl who'd lost her bus pass.

qa.q: What could help Gargi feel steadier about being in-between?
qa.a: Talking honestly with people like Sarika, and noticing both the grown-up things she handles and the help she still needs, without shame.

qa.q: How does Sarika see Gargi's worry?
qa.a: Sarika sees it as normal, sharing that at twenty-six she still calls Mummy about dal.

passage: Ayesha, you said you feel like a fake grown-up. Sit, and let your Avni Phuphi tell you about 1998. I was twenty-one, working my first job at a Delhi call centre, living in a working women's hostel. I paid my own rent and felt so independent. But every Sunday my father sent a parcel of food and an envelope of money, and I took it every time. One evening my roommate, Shabnam, found me crying over my first salary slip because it was less than Abbu earned when I was born. 'Are we adults or not?' I asked her. She laughed. 'We're both. Eat your parcel.' I decided then to stop asking. Three years later I tried to pay Abbu back for the envelopes. He tore up the cheque, and we both cried.

qa.q: Where did Avni live at twenty-one?
qa.a: In a working women's hostel in Delhi.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling crying over the first salary slip?
qa.a: Avni felt small and confused, comparing her pay to her father's and unsure whether she was really grown up.

qa.q: Avni decided to stop asking whether she was an adult yet. Why did that help?
qa.a: It let her accept being both independent and still supported, instead of feeling like a failure in between.

qa.q: How might Abbu have felt tearing up the cheque?
qa.a: Abbu probably felt proud and touched, and wanted Avni to know his help was never a debt.

grounding: An aunt recalls feeling half-independent and half-supported at twenty-one and learning that the in-between is normal.

passage: Losar was two days away, the Delhi winter fog thick outside the PG window, and Pema's train ticket home to Kalimpong was still waitlisted. Her part-time café wage covered food, not fares. She stared at her phone, thumb over Amala's name. Twenty-one, choosing her own courses, cooking her own dal, and still about to ask for ticket money. Her roommate Rajni, packing for Lohri at her own home, glanced up. "Just call." "It feels like admitting I'm a kid." "My dad still pays my phone bill," Rajni said. "I also fixed the landlord's leaking pipe myself last week. Nobody's fully one thing at our age." Pema laughed, a small surprised laugh, and pressed call. The fog didn't lift. But something in her chest did.

qa.q: Why was Pema's train ticket a problem?
qa.a: It was still waitlisted, and her café wage covered food, not fares.

qa.q: Why did calling Amala feel hard for Pema?
qa.a: Pema felt embarrassed and caught in between, independent in so many ways yet still needing help, as if asking meant admitting she was a kid.

qa.q: What helped Pema, and why?
qa.a: Rajni sharing her own mix of leaning on family and doing things alone made the in-between feeling seem normal 🙂, so Pema could make the call without shame.

qa.q: How does Rajni see their stage of life?
qa.a: Rajni sees it as normal to be part dependent and part grown up, like a dad paying the phone bill while fixing the pipe herself.
